title: Melt Spinning and Solution Spinning of Man-Made Fibres
description: Read article about This article explains melt and solution spinning of man-made fibres, comparing polymer behaviour, solidification, speed, cost, and effects on fibre properties. and more articles about Textile industary at Fibre2Fashion
head:
Key Takeaways
Melt spinning suits thermally stable polymers such as polyester, nylon, and polypropylene, offering the fastest, lowest-cost route because filaments solidify by cooling rather than solvent removal.
Solution spinning serves polymers that cannot form stable melts; dry spinning evaporates solvent, while wet spinning coagulates filaments in a bath and requires recovery.
markdown:
Introduction

Man-made fibres are produced by forcing a liquid polymer through the fine holes of a spinneret and then solidifying the emerging streams into filaments. This process is called spinning or extrusion. It differs from spinning in yarn manufacture, where staple fibres are twisted together.

The polymer must first be converted into a liquid or fluid state suitable for extrusion. Two principal routes are used: melt spinning, in which the polymer is melted, and solution spinning, in which the polymer is dissolved in a solvent. Solution spinning is broadly classified as dry spinning and wet spinning. The selection of the spinning route depends mainly on the thermal behaviour of the polymer.

Melt Spinning

Melt spinning is used for polymers that can be melted without decomposition. Important examples include polyester (PET), nylon 6, nylon 6,6 and polypropylene. The process converts polymer chips into a homogeneous melt, meters the melt through a spinneret, cools the extruded filaments and, where required, draws them to develop the required molecular orientation.

Figure 1: Melt Spinning Process

1. Process Sequence

1.  Drying and Melting. Polymer chips are dried and fed into a screw extruder, where they are melted. Drying is particularly important for polyester because moisture can cause hydrolysis and reduce molecular weight.

2. Metering and Filtration. A gear pump provides a controlled and constant melt flow. The melt passes through a filter pack that removes gels and particles that may block the spinneret or weaken the filaments.

3. Extrusion. The melt is forced through the spinneret. The number of holes determines the number of filaments, while the shape of the holes determines the filament cross-section. Common cross-sections include round, trilobal and hollow forms.

4. Quenching. The extruded filaments are cooled and solidified by controlled air flow in a quench chamber. Uniform cooling is necessary for consistent filament properties.

5. Finish Application and Take-Up. A spin finish is applied to control friction and static. The filaments are then guided over godet rollers and wound into packages.

6. Drawing. As-spun filaments may be stretched to several times their original length. Drawing increases molecular alignment along the fibre axis, increasing tenacity and reducing elongation. It may be carried out as a separate operation or integrated with spinning.

2. Spinning Speed and Yarn Forms

Take-up speed influences the molecular orientation of the as-spun yarn and therefore its subsequent processing requirements. Low-oriented yarn (LOY) is produced at lower speeds and requires full drawing. Partially oriented yarn (POY) is produced at higher speeds and is commonly used as feed yarn for draw-texturing. Fully drawn yarn (FDY) combines spinning and drawing in a continuous process.

3. Advantages and Limitation

Melt spinning does not require a solvent, eliminating solvent recovery from the spinning process. It is the fastest and lowest-cost route among the three principal methods considered here. Its main limitation is that it can be used only with polymers that remain thermally stable at their melting temperature.

Solution Spinning

Solution spinning is used when a polymer cannot be melted without decomposition. The polymer is dissolved in a suitable solvent to form a viscous spinning solution, or dope. The extruded filament is solidified by removing the solvent. The mechanism of solvent removal distinguishes dry spinning from wet spinning.

1. Dry Spinning

In dry spinning, the polymer dope contains a volatile solvent. The dope is extruded into a heated chamber through which hot air or an inert gas flows. The solvent evaporates and the filament solidifies. The solvent vapour is recovered for reuse.

Figure 2: Dry Spinning Process

Typical dry-spun fibres include cellulose acetate, triacetate, some acrylic fibres and elastane (spandex). Because solidification begins at the filament surface, the cross-section may become non-circular. Acetate fibres can show a lobed outline, while dry-spun acrylic may develop a dog-bone shape.

Dry spinning is slower than melt spinning because solvent evaporation controls solidification. Solvent recovery also increases process cost and requires appropriate safety and environmental controls.

2. Wet Spinning

In wet spinning, the spinneret is placed directly in a coagulation bath. The extruded filaments solidify through solvent exchange or chemical reaction and are subsequently washed, drawn, finished and dried. The product may be wound as continuous filament or cut into staple fibre.

Figure 3: Wet Spinning Process

Viscose rayon is a major example. Cellulose is converted to sodium cellulose xanthate and dissolved in dilute sodium hydroxide. The resulting dope is extruded into an acid bath, usually containing sulphuric acid, sodium sulphate and zinc sulphate, where cellulose is regenerated. The serrated cross-section of viscose is associated with skin formation and shrinkage during regeneration.

Acrylic fibres may also be wet spun using solvents such as dimethylformamide (DMF) or dimethylacetamide (DMAc), and modacrylic fibres are also produced by this route.

Wet spinning is the slowest of the three principal methods because coagulation involves chemical and diffusion processes. It also requires substantial liquid handling for coagulation, washing and chemical recovery.

3. Dry-Jet Wet Spinning

Dry-jet wet spinning places the spinneret a short distance above the coagulation bath. The extruded filament passes through a small air gap before entering the bath. This arrangement permits higher drawing and improved molecular orientation. The method is used for high-performance fibres such as para-aramid fibres, including Kevlar, spun from concentrated sulphuric acid, and lyocell, spun from N-methylmorpholine-N-oxide (NMMO).

4. Gel Spinning

Gel spinning is a solution-based method used for ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) fibres such as Dyneema and Spectra. A dilute polymer solution is extruded and cooled to form a gel filament. The filament is then drawn to very high ratios, producing fibres with very high strength and modulus.

Comparing the Spinning Methods

The three principal routes differ in polymer state, solidification mechanism, processing speed, cost and solvent requirements. These differences determine the suitability of each method for a particular polymer and end-use requirement.

| Feature | Melt spinning | Dry spinning | Wet spinning |
| Polymer state | Melt | Solution | Solution |
| Solidification | Cooling | Solvent evaporation | Coagulation in bath |
| Solvent recovery | None | Required | Required |
| Relative speed | Highest | Intermediate | Lowest |
| Relative cost | Lowest | Higher | Higher |
| Examples | Polyester, nylon, polypropylene | Acetate, triacetate, elastane, some acrylic | Viscose, acrylic, modacrylic |

Table 1: Comparison of Melt, Dry and Wet Spinning.

Influence of Spinning Method on Fibre Properties

The spinning route affects fibre structure as well as production conditions. The final properties are determined by the interaction between extrusion, solidification, spinning speed and drawing.

•   Cross-Section: In melt spinning, the spinneret hole is the main control over filament cross-section. In solution spinning, the solidification mechanism also influences the final shape.

•   Internal Structure: Wet-spun fibres such as viscose may develop a skin–core structure during coagulation and regeneration, influencing strength and dyeing behaviour.

•   Void Content: Some solution-spun fibres can contain voids, which influence lustre and dye uptake.

•   Orientation and Crystallinity: Across the three methods, molecular orientation and crystallinity are influenced by spinning speed and the extent of drawing after extrusion.

Melt spinning is the preferred route for polymers that can be melted without degradation because it is fast, comparatively simple and does not require solvents. Solution spinning is required when the polymer cannot be processed as a stable melt. Dry spinning removes solvent by evaporation, whereas wet spinning solidifies the filament through coagulation in a bath. Dry-jet wet spinning and gel spinning extend solution-based processing to fibres requiring high molecular orientation or very high strength.

Thus, the choice of spinning method is determined primarily by polymer behaviour during processing, while the selected solidification mechanism and subsequent drawing conditions influence filament structure and properties.
